newsitem.title: BELGIUM: New Labour faces battle over British beef ban.
newsitem.headline: New Labour faces battle over British beef ban.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government, which has pledged a constructive approach towards the Europe Union, faces a tough test in convincing its partners to ease a world ban on British beef exports.
European Union diplomats and officials said the embargo was aimed at protecting consumer health and could not be lifted simply to satisfy political objectives.
Britain's new agriculture minister, Jack Cunningham, is likely to be given this message when he meets EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler in a get-to-know-you meeting in Brussels on Monday.

The ban was imposed by the European Union in March 1996 after the former Conservative government said mad cow disease, or bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), could be transmitted to humans. BSE has struck mainly British cattle.
"It's a health issue, not a political matter," said one diplomat, noting that Britain agreed last June to strict terms for a phased lifting of the ban at an EU summit in Florence.
Britain's policy of blocking EU business in order to force concessions on the beef ban ahead of the Florence meeting was seen as inflaming political tensions.
"Nothing has really changed," said another diplomat, adding there was more likely to be a shift in style than substance.

The EU's executive Commission, under pressure from the European Parliament for mishandling the BSE crisis, has stressed that public health must be given priority and is tightening food safety measures.
"We have always argued against politicising the beef ban and said that any action on BSE would be decided on the basis of scientific evidence," Commission agriculture spokesman Gerard Kiely said.
"That's the basis on which the Commission has worked and will continue to work," he added.

Recent EU inspections and a report last week by the New Scientist magazine that mad cow disease may be quietly spreading across Europe because farmers and veterinarians are failing to report sick cows have raised pressure for more anti-BSE action.
That is likely to make Brussels even more cautious about any early relaxation of the British beef ban, diplomats said.
In February, Britain proposed as a first step the setting up a "certified herd scheme" to identify cows from BSE-free herds which could then be exported.
Last month Fischler and EU food safety commissioner Emma Bonino questioned how the complex scheme would work in the absence of computer records in England, Scotland and Wales.
It would only be practical for home-bred animals or for herds where there had been few cattle movements, they said.
But they added that the scheme would be easier to apply in Northern Ireland where a computerised cattle tracking system was introduced in 1988.

EU scientists are due to give their opinion on the British proposal by the end of May. It will then be discussed by the EU's Standing Veterinary Committee of senior member state officials after which the Commission would take a decision.
